analysis.one_liner: Removes Medicare's exclusion of hearing aid coverage and requires a federal study of hearing aid assistance programs.
analysis.headline: The bill to cover hearing aids under Medicare was introduced with 10 cosponsors from both parties and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare does not pay for hearing aids. This bill would strike the line in law that excludes hearing aids and the exams for them from Medicare coverage, starting January 1, 2024. It would also order the Government Accountability Office to study existing programs that help people get hearing aids and report back to Congress. The bill was never voted on in committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Older adults on Medicare with hearing loss, who today pay out of pocket for hearing aids that commonly cost thousands of dollars per pair. It would also benefit audiologists and hearing aid providers by making hearing care billable under Medicare. [S2]

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the statutory exclusion at Section 1862(a)(7) of the Social Security Act, so Medicare would cover hearing aids and the examinations for them. [S2]
Sets the coverage change to take effect for items and services on or after January 1, 2024. [S3]
Directs the Comptroller General to study federal programs and health insurance coverage for hearing aids and report to Congress with recommendations within 18 months of the effective date. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Medicare (the federal government and taxpayers) pays the cost of hearing aids and exams, and beneficiaries' monthly premiums could rise to reflect the new benefit. Hearing aid makers and dispensers gain a large new payer.

drawbacks.text: The Congressional Budget Office and CRS materials provided do not estimate the cost, but adding hearing aid coverage to Medicare adds federal spending at a time when Medicare's finances are a recurring concern; critics would have to weigh that against beneficiaries' out-of-pocket savings. [S2]

The bill removes the statutory exclusion but does not itself spell out payment rates or utilization controls, so details like provider payment levels would be left to Medicare administrative rulemaking. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance the bill would shift thousands of dollars in out-of-pocket costs away from older Americans and toward Medicare, a fairly standard expansion of a health benefit, with the main cost being federal spending and premiums and the main design question being how payment details get filled in later. The hearing aid industry benefits alongside beneficiaries rather than being entrenched as a gatekeeper, since the bill simply adds coverage rather than routing a new public program through private intermediaries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and sat there without a markup or floor vote through the end of the Congress in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced January 10, 2023 by Rep. Debbie Dingell with bipartisan original cosponsors including Rep. Fitzpatrick. [S1]
Referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means. [S5]
Referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on January 20, 2023, and referred to that subcommittee again on December 17, 2024, with no markup or vote in between. [S5]
No further action by the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries with hearing loss are no better off, since coverage never arrived. Industries that profit from today's exclusion, including hearing aid dispensers, and members of Congress who did not have to find offsets for a new benefit, are better off because the bill died in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hearing aid dispensers and the status quo

industries.note: The bill would make hearing aids billable under Medicare, creating a large new payer for their products and services. Their gain comes from expanded coverage, not from charging beneficiaries more. [S2]

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage and supplemental insurance plans
industries.note: Some plans today offer limited hearing aid benefits as an extra. A universal statutory benefit could reduce the appeal of that added coverage. The sources provided do not discuss this industry, so this is general context rather than a sourced claim.
